bears.note: Pico presents the Heptaplus as a gift to Lorenzo, whose leisure at Fiesole made it possible.
Poliziano is described as a constant visitor during the writing of the Heptaplus.
Lorenzo supplied the retreat at Fiesole.

judged.justification: Grounds the reading of the surface of Moses as a veil for a hidden philosophy.
Shows Pico treating Dionysius as a disciple of Paul who reports apostolic esoteric practice, the stance he takes in the Third Exposition.

open.t: The proem defers any use of the Hebrew authorities; how far the Heptaplus later draws on them is left for the reader to check against the text.

judged.justification: Pico says he sets aside the Chaldean and Hebrew commentators and claims the seven interpretations as his own invention.
Fixes Pico's own equation of the angelic world with the philosophers' intelligible world.

quotes.t: This is the world of darkness; that the world of light; the heavens are compounded of light and darkness.
of a middle nature, the heavens are on that account called by the Hebrews asciamaim, as if composed of es and maim, that is, of the fire and water of which we spoke.

judged.justification: A location claim (no sin above the moon) that Pico states without discussion, relevant to the trial articles on where angels dwell.
Pico himself names mutual containment as the hinge of the whole work; the fourfold and later expositions are derived from it.

open.t: Pico names no text for the attribution to Anaxagoras beyond the Pythagoreans and Platonists who expound him.

wallis1965-heptaplus:019.hedge_words: If we have understood him rightly, I believe

judged.justification: Identifies the seraphic intellect with fire and love in the intelligible world by an explicit three-tier analogy.

quotes.t: There is water in our world; there is water in the heavens, the mover and mistress of ours, namely, the moon, the vestibule of the heavens
the heavens, the waters are the minds of the cherubim.
the elemental moisture quenches the heat of life; the celestial feeds it; the supercelestial understands it.

judged.justification: Ties the cherubic order to understanding by the same analogy.
States the nine orders and God as primal unity in the terms used later in the Third Exposition.
Makes the cosmology the ground of the hermeneutics.

open.t: Whether 'angelic mind' here names a faculty of the human soul distinct from 'reason' is not explained in this passage.

judged.justification: The angelic mind is listed as a component of man, as a school commonplace, not as a doctrine Pico argues here.

open.t: The proem lists the angelic world first, but the contents give the elemental world first and the angelic third; the source states both orders and does not reconcile them.

judged.justification: The proem lists the angelic world first; the contents put the elemental world first and the angelic third.

quotes.t: We shall not, however, imitate those who, having tried sometimes to explain the creation of the world, have heaped together whatever philosophers or theologians have anywhere said about God, the angels, matter, the heavens, and the whole of nature. Among …

judged.justification: States that the Heptaplus is meant to be brief on angels and other topics and to rely on the reader's prior learning.
The seven are the seven expositions, each with seven chapters; nothing here describes seven interpretive layers within each exposition.

open.t: Pico cites Simeon without a passage; an editorial note in the source points to the Zohar (I, 16a) at the parallel place, but the gate does not allow that note as a claim.

judged.justification: A rare place where the Zohar's author is invoked for a doctrinal point alongside the Peripatetics, in the elemental exposition.
Saturn is glossed as the union of the intelligible world, the angelic realm of the second proem, which bears on the Commento's Saturn.
Shows the direction of dependence Pico assumes between Plato and Hebrew learning.
Claims novelty for the reading in which one text serves all four worlds.
Pico cites Dionysius and Aquinas together as authorities on angelic knowledge, before the Third Exposition.

quotes.t: This Isaac takes the tenth sphere to be what Ezekiel designated as the sapphire in the likeness of a throne, since the color of the sapphire signifies the splendor of its light, the likeness to a throne its immobility.

judged.justification: A case where 'throne' names an unmoving heaven, not an angelic order.

open.t: Pico leaves undecided whether the empyrean, which he compares to the unity presiding over the nine spheres, is corporeal.

wallis1965-heptaplus:047.hedge_words: Some doubt whether its nature be corporeal or not rather incorporeal

judged.justification: Angels are called gods by participation, and God stands to the nine choirs as the empyrean to the nine spheres: the analogy of the second proem restated.
Makes the empyrean the seat of spirits, while the Third Exposition reads the same words of the angelic intellect and of love.
Pico takes the 'man' of the sixth day as the rational soul of the heavens in this exposition.

open.t: Pico gives no argument here for the identity of nature of good and evil angels; the claim is asserted as a scriptural usage.

judged.justification: A flat statement that the evil demon does not differ in nature from the good angels, offered as an ordinary scriptural usage.
An instance of Pico supplying a rationale for a Hebrew dogma that his sources leave unexplained.
Human souls are of the same stuff as the celestial souls and higher than the heavens, a premise for the Third Exposition's ranking of man against angels.

quotes.t: Since much about the angelic and invisible nature has been handed down by the ancient Hebrews and much also by Dionysius, it was my plan to expound the words of Moses according to the teaching of both schools.

judged.justification: Pico himself names two separate schools of angelology, Hebrew and Dionysian, and says he planned to use both; the Heptaplus's Third Exposition is therefore presented as only half the plan.

open.t: Which work Pico means by writing 'more fully elsewhere' is not named in the passage.

judged.justification: Postpones the Hebrew angelology to another work; the Heptaplus's Third Exposition is deliberately Dionysian.
States the concordist test Pico proposes to apply to Hebrew material.
Pico places the Dionysian corpus in an apostolic line (Hierotheus, Paul, Dionysius) and chooses it as the guide of the Third Exposition.
Pico himself labels the treatment of angels by number and unity Pythagorean; it ties the angelology to the doctrine of unity that later figures in the dispute over the One.
God is being itself and unity itself in this exposition, which bears on how Pico later states the convertibility of being and one.
Angel as number (multiplicity in one respect, unity in another) is Pico's structure for angelic nature.
States an essence-being composition and a distinction of intellect from its act in angels, in a passage that says nothing of matter.
Applies the 'earth' of Genesis to angelic essence, as a created and initially unformed substrate of multiplicity.
Makes love, not knowledge, the movement by which the angelic intellect is turned to God and lit; understanding precedes love.

quotes.t: God said "Be light made," and light was made in the angel, the light of intelligible forms
let this reason be enough for us-that intelligible species are united to angelic minds by eternal links and an indivisible bond, not a vague and customary one as happens with the human intellect.

judged.justification: Places the three Dionysian hierarchies in the Genesis text and gives them locations relative to the heavens.

quotes.t: All this, if we consider the nature and duties of the three hierarchies, could not be more in accord with the teaching of Dionysius. Since, as he writes, the highest hierarchy has leisure only for contemplation, it is properly symbolized …

judged.justification: Says the first hierarchy is purely contemplative and the second governs the heavens; the orders within them are not named here.

open.t: The Third Exposition names the orders of only the third hierarchy; the assignment of the other six orders is not given in the passage.

judged.justification: Only the lowest hierarchy's three orders are named in this exposition; seraphim, cherubim and thrones are not mentioned in the exposition's scheme of hierarchies.

quotes.t: What it may be for the waters under the heavens to be gathered together into one place would perhaps be doubtful if it were not explained to us by Paul, in whom we read that the angels sent to carry …
From this we can understand that these subcelestial waters, that is, the angelic armies, have been assembled into one place to look after the good and salvation of man alone.

judged.justification: Angels as governors of particular bodies, with Augustine and Gregory as authority, bears on the location and function questions.
Records Pico's report of a view on the rank of the sinning angel.

open.t: Pico calls the contemplative hierarchy the third here, although in chapter 3 he counts it the first; the source uses both orders without comment.

judged.justification: Angels are identified with the movers of the stars and the illuminators of human souls.

quotes.t: since, as Dionysius says, there are three angelic activities, purification, illumination, and perfection, they are so distributed that the lowest order purifies, the highest perfects, and the middle one, which we are now discussing, illuminates.
the heavenly ones illuminate it when purified; the super celestial ones perfect it with a fiery and life-giving dew

judged.justification: Ties the orders to a triad of purgation, illumination, perfection as in the Oration, with the highest order 'fiery' (fire, seraph) and the lowest purgative.
A place where the Hebrew reading is used positively for the angelic host, in an exposition otherwise on Dionysian lines.

quotes.t: Prophet refutes the error of the philosophers who believed that there are certain princely intellectual substances but denied that each of them is set over a numerous multitude of lower rank, like the commander of a legion, as the theologians …

Since we know of nine orders of angels, and since each order has chosen its own leader by lot, let us fashion that leader and prince in our minds as a great sphere, and then the following army as the …

open.t: Pico does not name the philosophers who denied that each princely substance heads a multitude.

judged.justification: Nine orders, each with a leader over a multitude, imaged by spheres: a structural picture of the angelic world; the philosophers whose error is refuted are not named.
Man is neither an angel nor part of the angelic hierarchy, but its terminus; contrast the second proem's 'angelic mind' as one of man's components.
Ranks Christ's humanity above the angels by appeal to Dionysius and Paul and says men can be raised above the angels through grace.
Locates the human share in the angelic mind in an intelligence above reason.

Says the illuminating intellect is called the Spirit of the Lord by Jewish philosophers and Alfarabi, tying the Agent Intellect to the Genesis text, and reports a split between God and an intermediate mind.
Rejects a view of Maimonides and Abubacher on the conjunction of the separate intellect.

open.t: Pico does not name the recent philosophers or state the controversy, and defers the point.

judged.justification: Pico says he is in a controversy over the identification of the active intellect and declines to use it here.
Explains why the Fifth Exposition reads the sequence of the days as a sequence of worlds, angelic first.

open.t: Pico does not say whether he adopts the theory that 'intellect' is unworthy of God, nor whom he means by those who hold it.

judged.justification: Reports and appears to explain a theory that calls 'intellect' unworthy of God, bearing on the question of the One beyond intellect and being.

open.t: The passage does not say what the act and the potency are in an angel; the relation to the essence and being distinction of the Third Exposition is not stated.

judged.justification: Pico accepts the act-and-potency composition of angels as a common doctrine while refusing to settle the disputed terms.
The Fifth Exposition reads heaven and earth as act and potency in angels, where the Third Exposition read them as being and essence.
Sets the concordist project of reconciling Plato and Aristotle as the planned work into which philosophical detail is deferred.

bears.note: Pico names Ficino 'our friend' and looks forward to his Latin Plotinus with commentary.

judged.justification: Pico calls Ficino his friend and anticipates his Latin Plotinus in the Heptaplus.

open.t: The second proem calls man 'a fourth world'; the Fifth Exposition says he is 'not so much a fourth world' as their bond; the source states both without reconciling them.

judged.justification: Qualifies the second proem's description of man as a fourth world.
Man's containing of all natures is put as distinct from the angelic containing of things by knowing them.
Repeats the better-stamp / degenerate contrast of the second proem for the case of man.

open.t: The text does not say whether 'participation in the angelic mind' means sharing an intellect or a capacity for angelic knowing.

judged.justification: Man participates in the angelic mind; this is the phrase Pico's later writing might be compared with.

wallis1965-heptaplus:105.hedge_words: if what Paul writes is true

judged.justification: Assigns fallen angels a role as executioners in the cosmic commonwealth.
Identifies the One with the Trinity in the Heptaplus's account of unity, relevant to the later exchange about the One and Being.
Says the Spirit of God, read in us as the intellect, is joined to bodies as an art to its matter, the language used of a separate intellect.
States that the human intellect is to be joined to the first intellect.
Ties One to beginning and Good to end, and attributes the pair to the Pythagoreans, in the work's closing account of felicity.

quotes.t: In fact, even to the angels, whom they call minds and intellects, and whose supreme perfection they acknowledge because the angels understand God, they ascribe no further knowledge of God than that by which angels know themselves, so that the …

judged.justification: Pico reports a limit on angelic knowledge of God that he then says only grace overcomes.
Pico grades the active-intellect theories as adequate only to natural felicity.
Puts angels, as well as men, in need of grace to reach the beatific vision and links the sin of Lucifer to trying to ascend by one's own power.
Restates the angel-as-number teaching of the Third Exposition for man: return from multiplicity to unity, and calls God 'the One'.

open.t: The Seventh Exposition again assigns 'heaven' and 'earth' to new referents (angels and men); the source reads the same words differently in each exposition, as the second proem announces.

judged.justification: Here 'heaven' means the angelic nature and 'earth' the human, as opposed to the readings of the Third and Fifth Expositions.
Places demons in the air and says an angel gave the law to Moses.
Shows Pico using Hebrew sources polemically, in his own words as weapons against the Hebrews.
Calls the sevenfold interpretation complete and treats the first phrase as a separate, additional method.
Gives Pico's own account of the letter-permutation method and its authority.

open.t: Pico names no supporters of the permutation method in this passage.

wallis1965-heptaplus:129.hedge_words: I cannot prove or demonstrate what I claim

judged.justification: Pico himself states the limits of his warrant for the Hebrew permutation method.
The Hebrew phrase is resolved into a Trinitarian statement and a description of the great man.

quotes.t: In the first place, therefore, it should be noticed that the world is what Moses calls "the great man." For if man is a little world, then certainly the world is a great man.

Likewise in the world the highest part, which is the angelic or intellectual world, is the fountain of knowledge, because that nature was made for understanding. The middle part, which is the sky, is the principle of life, motion, and …

judged.justification: Maps the three worlds onto head, breast and lower body, so that the angelic world is the intellect of the great man.

open.t: The note leaves the identity of Eleazar open, and Garin's identifications are suggestions.

quotes.t: Pseudo-Dionysius, Caelestis hierarchia VII; Aquinas, Summa theologica, I, q. 89, a. 1.

judged.justification: Gives the editors' source references for the Dionysius and Thomas authority on angelic knowledge.

quotes.t: Fictitious mystic referred to as historical by the Pseudo-Dionysius.

judged.justification: States that the mystic whom Pico says Dionysius followed is a fiction of the Dionysian corpus.
Editors flag that Pico's phrase for the evil demon rests on the Latin inimicus homo.

open.t: The note says the source of the Chaldean saying is not given by Pico.
The note says no source is given for the saying attributed to the Saracens.
